title: He that dwelleth (Psalm 90 [91])
hookLine: under his wings, and angels to keep thee in all thy ways

lines: TWO CHILDREN ON A BROKEN BRIDGE.
cards: If you grew up Catholic, there may have been a small picture over your bed: two children crossing a rickety bridge over a gorge at night, planks broken, water rushing below, and behind them, huge and gentle, an angel with its wings spread, keeping them from falling.
Sentimental, maybe. But the idea behind it is old and serious, and a lot of it comes from one psalm, a psalm the devil himself once quoted.

teach.h: UNDER HIS WINGS THOU SHALT TRUST.
teach.b: Psalm 90 in the Douay, 91 in most Bibles: "He that dwelleth in the aid of the most High, shall abide under the protection of the God of Jacob."
Then a mother bird: "He will overshadow thee with his shoulders: and under his wings thou shalt trust."
Then the fears: the terror of the night, the arrow that flies by day, the thing that walks about in the dark, the noonday devil.
And then: "For he hath given his angels charge over thee; to keep thee in all thy ways. In their hands they shall bear thee up: lest thou dash thy foot against a stone."
Here's where the devil comes in. In the desert, Matthew says, the tempter took Jesus to the top of the Temple, quoted these lines, and said: jump. The angels will catch you.
Scripture, used as bait. Jesus answered with other scripture: "Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God." The psalm is a promise of care, not a dare.
From this psalm, and from Jesus's words that children's angels always see the face of his Father in heaven, the Church draws its teaching on guardian angels.
The Catechism says that beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd, and that human life, from its beginning until death, is surrounded by the angels' care.

Catholics keep a feast of the guardian angels on October 2, and there's a short traditional prayer to one's angel, the kind children learn by heart. It's also the Church's Sunday night psalm, at Compline.
The week ran from a thirsty deer to be still, a clean heart, a morning thirst, a sparrow's home and numbered days, and ends here: under his wings.

how: Catholics pray Psalm 90 [91] at Night Prayer on Sundays and on the first Sunday of Lent, when the Gospel tells of the temptation in the desert; some pray daily to their guardian angel, and the Church keeps the feast of the Guardian Angels on October 2.

o: a loved one who died and now watches over you
an angel beside each believer, a protector for life
a saint you pick at confirmation to pray to

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.
p: to keep thee in all thy ways
quoted the psalm and said jump
the feast of the Guardian Angels

s: the devil quotes this psalm to Jesus in Matthew's Gospel
on the pinnacle of the Temple: the angels will bear thee up.
the Catechism says only saints have guardian angels
it teaches that every believer has an angel as protector and shepherd.
the psalm is a dare to take risks and see if God catches you
Jesus answers: thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God. it's a promise, not a dare.

games.q: you're Jesus on the top of the Temple. the tempter quotes this psalm: jump, the angels will catch you. what do you do?
o: jump, to prove the psalm true.
answer with scripture: thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.
argue about what the psalm means.
games.why: Jesus answered, it is written again: thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God. the promise of care isn't something to test.

practice: Think of your own rickety bridge this week, whatever feels unsteady, and something large and gentle behind you, wings open, not stopping you from walking, just keeping you from falling.
If you pray, speak to your guardian angel in your own words, or with the traditional prayer to the guardian angel; if you don't, rest in the picture of being kept.

wordCard.voice: Guardian angel. The angel Catholics believe stands beside each believer, as protector and shepherd, from the beginning of life until death. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: messenger. the New Testament's word for angel.

carryVoice: Your line: under his wings. The bridge is still yours to walk. A week of psalms, done.
